title: A cross-sectional look at teacher reactions, worries, and professional development needs related to generative AI in an urban school district
extended_summary:
This paper examines how K-12 teachers in a large urban school district reacted to the rapid emergence of generative AI tools such as ChatGPT, with a focus on their concerns, perceived benefits, and professional development needs. The authors ask whether teachers’ views differ by grade level, subject area, and years of teaching experience, and whether those characteristics shape willingness to allow student use of AI for different academic tasks.

The study uses a cross-sectional mixed-methods survey of 1,454 certificated educators in one large urban district on the U.S. West Coast. Teachers reported on prior chatbot use, allowability of several AI uses (idea generation, paper editing/completion, full paper writing, concept explanation, and code generation), open-ended concerns and benefits for teachers versus students, and desired professional learning topics. Quantitative analyses included logistic regression and chi-square tests, while open-ended responses were coded thematically.

Findings show a strong grade-level pattern: teachers in higher grades were less willing to allow AI chatbot use than elementary teachers, with high school teachers especially focused on guarding against misuse. More experienced teachers were generally more restrictive, particularly in humanities. Across the sample, teachers worried more about student overreliance and plagiarism than about their own use, while perceived benefits also differed by whether AI was being considered for teachers or students. Professional development needs varied by grade level: elementary and middle school teachers wanted basic AI literacy, whereas high school teachers emphasized guidance on student use and detecting AI-generated work. The authors conclude that AI professional development and policy should be targeted by grade level and teaching context rather than treated as one-size-fits-all.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: Generic generative AI chatbot technology used for conversational text generation and related academic tasks; the paper references tools such as ChatGPT but does not evaluate a different named product beyond that example.
identified_tools.use_case: Teachers were surveyed about their reactions, concerns, allowability policies, benefits, and professional development needs regarding generative AI chatbots in K-12 schools, with ChatGPT used as the exemplar in survey wording.

findings.finding_summary: In a mixed-methods survey of 1,454 teachers in a large urban district, teachers in higher grade levels were less willing to allow student use of generative AI chatbots. The paper reports decreasing likelihood of allowability from elementary to middle to high school across idea generation, paper editing, full-paper writing, concept explanation, and code generation (e.g., marginal effects of about -0.121 to -0.150 across outcomes).
findings.measure: Teacher allowability/policy responses for five chatbot uses

findings.finding_summary: For elementary teachers, those with more than 10 years of experience were substantially less likely to allow student use for writing support tasks. The reported marginal effects were -0.489 for generating ideas, -0.502 for editing a paper, and -0.587 for writing an entire paper (all p<0.05), indicating stronger resistance among more experienced elementary teachers.
findings.measure: Teacher allowability for writing-support uses of AI chatbots by experience level
findings.sample_size: n=113 to n=115 depending on outcome

findings.finding_summary: Among high school teachers, more experienced humanities and STEM teachers were more likely to disallow AI chatbot use for writing support, with significant negative marginal effects for idea generation and paper editing. For example, more experienced humanities teachers had dy/dx=-0.329 for idea generation and -0.378 for paper editing, while more experienced STEM teachers had dy/dx=-0.404 for paper editing; the paper notes no significant model result for code generation at alpha=0.05.
findings.measure: Teacher allowability for AI chatbot writing-support uses by grade level, subject, and experience
findings.sample_size: n=69 to n=97 depending on outcome

findings.finding_summary: Teachers’ concerns and perceived benefits differed significantly when considering AI use by teachers versus students. For concerns, overreliance was most frequently cited for students (29.52%) and teachers (18.21%), plagiarism/misuse was much more common as a student concern (26.35%) than a teacher concern (3.35%), and misinformation was more often a concern for teachers (13.58%) than students (3.17%).
findings.measure: Open-ended concern codes for teacher vs student AI use
findings.sample_size: n=668 to n=669 depending on question

findings.finding_summary: Teachers also viewed benefits differently for themselves and students. For teachers, the most common benefits were insufficient personal knowledge about AI (22.16%), lesson planning/materials (21.41%), and increased efficiency (13.62%); for students, the most common benefit was information retrieval (20.33%), followed by other uncoded benefits (22.57%) and insufficient personal knowledge about AI (22.42%).
findings.measure: Open-ended benefit codes for teacher vs student AI use
findings.sample_size: n=626 to n=630 depending on question

findings.finding_summary: Professional development needs varied significantly by grade level (chi-square p<0.001) but not by subject or experience level. Elementary and middle school teachers more often wanted basic AI introductions, while high school teachers more often wanted training on how to instruct/manage student AI use and how to detect AI-generated work.
findings.measure: Professional development needs from open-ended survey responses

quality_tier_rationale: This is a single-district mixed-methods survey study with descriptive coding and regression analyses, not an experimental evaluation. It provides useful correlational evidence about teacher perceptions and setting-specific variation, but causal inference is limited.
impact_tier_rationale: The study reports substantial differences in teacher allowability and PD needs across grade levels and experience groups, but it does not estimate student learning gains or other direct outcome effects. Reported effects are mostly marginal effects in policy/attitude models rather than educational impact on achievement.
